text: Out-tree down, in-tree up; ranges = O(log n) nodes.

Segment-tree graph building (线段树优化建图): edges "from u to every vertex in [l, r]" (or the reverse) would cost O(n) edges each. Build two segment trees whose nodes are extra vertices: an out-tree with edges parent → child (weight 0), whose leaves are the real vertices, and an in-tree with edges child → parent (weight 0). Then u → [l, r] is u → the O(log n) covering nodes of the out-tree; [l, r] → u goes from the covering nodes of the in-tree to u.

O((n + m log n)) edges in total, then any graph algorithm runs as usual (Dijkstra here, CF786B Legacy; also SCC and 2-SAT). The leaves of both trees must be the same real vertices (or joined by 0-edges), so paths can enter one tree and leave the other.

Prefix variables P_i; O(k) clauses per group.

2-SAT with "at most one" groups: forbidding every pair inside a group of size k costs O(k²) clauses. Add prefix variables Pi = "some of the first i members is true". Clauses: xi → Pi, Pi−1 → Pi, and Pi−1 → ¬xi (if an earlier member is true, xi must be false). O(k) clauses, the same answers (Riddle P6378).
The same prefix trick (or a segment tree over the literals, 23.1) shrinks any "range of implications" in 2- SAT. Solve with SCCs as in 进阶篇第12章 : unsatisfiable iff some x and ¬x share an SCC.

Potentials from Bellman-Ford; Dijkstra n times.

Johnson's algorithm (Johnson 全源最短路) finds all-pairs shortest paths with negative edges (but no negative cycle) in O(nm log m), better than Floyd's O(n³) on sparse graphs. Add a virtual vertex 0 with 0- edges to all vertices; Bellman-Ford / SPFA gives potentials h(v) = dist(0, v). Reweight w'(u, v) = w(u, v) + h(u) − h(v) ≥ 0, run Dijkstra from every vertex, and undo: dist(u, v) = dist'(u, v) − h(u) + h(v).

Why reweighting keeps shortest paths: along any path u → v the potentials telescope, so every path's length changes by the same h(u) − h(v). And w' ≥ 0 because h(v) ≤ h(u) + w(u, v) (the triangle inequality of shortest distances). A negative cycle shows up in the Bellman-Ford step (P5905).

The Luogu problems for this chapter, a ladder through them, and experiments to try yourself.
Key points to memorise
1. Out-tree: parent → child 0-edges; u → range = u → covering nodes.
2. In-tree: child → parent 0-edges; range → u = covering nodes → u.
3. At most one per group: P_i ⇐ x_i, P_i ⇐ P_(i−1), P_(i−1) ⇒ ¬x_i.
4. Johnson: h from Bellman-Ford; w' = w + h(u) − h(v) ≥ 0; undo after Dijkstra.
